label: Adaptability
entry_text: Adaptability is the capacity to adjust one's methods or behavior when requirements, circumstances, or available information change.
example: When a venue becomes unavailable, an organizer redesigns the event for a smaller room without dropping its essential activities.

label: Arm-Hand Steadiness
entry_text: The ability to keep your hand and arm steady while moving your arm or while holding your arm and hand in one position.

label: Attention to detail
entry_text: Attention to detail is the capacity to notice and verify small elements whose omission or inconsistency could affect the result.
example: A payroll reviewer catches a transposed digit in an employee's recorded hours before the payment goes out.

label: Auditory Attention
entry_text: The ability to focus on a single source of sound in the presence of other distracting sounds.

label: Category Flexibility
entry_text: The ability to generate or use different sets of rules for combining or grouping things in different ways.

label: Causal reasoning
entry_text: Causal reasoning is the ability to judge whether a change or event produces an outcome rather than merely accompanying it.
example: An analyst compares randomly assigned groups to determine whether a new reminder actually increased attendance.

label: Control Precision
entry_text: The ability to quickly and repeatedly adjust the controls of a machine or a vehicle to exact positions.

label: Deductive Reasoning
entry_text: The ability to apply general rules to specific problems to produce answers that make sense.

label: Depth Perception
entry_text: The ability to judge which of several objects is closer or farther away from you, or to judge the distance between you and an object.

label: Dynamic Flexibility
entry_text: The ability to quickly and repeatedly bend, stretch, twist, or reach out with your body, arms, and/or legs.

label: Dynamic Strength
entry_text: The ability to exert muscle force repeatedly or continuously over time. This involves muscular endurance and resistance to muscle fatigue.

label: Emotional stability
entry_text: Emotional stability is a tendency to maintain relatively steady emotional responses and recover composure under stress.
example: A dispatcher remains composed during a surge of calls and continues applying the same triage criteria.
sense_note: Better understood as a disposition than as a discrete cognitive ability.

label: Explosive Strength
entry_text: The ability to use short bursts of muscle force to propel oneself (as in jumping or sprinting), or to throw an object.

label: Extent Flexibility
entry_text: The ability to bend, stretch, twist, or reach with your body, arms, and/or legs.

label: Far Vision
entry_text: The ability to see details at a distance.

label: Finger Dexterity
entry_text: The ability to make precisely coordinated movements of the fingers of one or both hands to grasp, manipulate, or assemble very small objects.

label: Flexibility of Closure
entry_text: The ability to identify or detect a known pattern (a figure, object, word, or sound) that is hidden in other distracting material.

label: Fluency of Ideas
entry_text: The ability to come up with a number of ideas about a topic (the number of ideas is important, not their quality, correctness, or creativity).

label: Glare Sensitivity
entry_text: The ability to see objects in the presence of a glare or bright lighting.

label: Goal-oriented
entry_text: Being goal-oriented is a tendency to organize and prioritize work around a specified objective.
example: A tutor uses the student's target reading level to choose exercises and measure progress each week.
sense_note: The adjectival label describes a work orientation.

label: Gross Body Coordination
entry_text: The ability to coordinate the movement of your arms, legs, and torso together when the whole body is in motion.

label: Gross Body Equilibrium
entry_text: The ability to keep or regain your body balance or stay upright when in an unstable position.

label: Hearing Sensitivity
entry_text: The ability to detect or tell the differences between sounds that vary in pitch and loudness.

label: Inductive Reasoning
entry_text: The ability to combine pieces of information to form general rules or conclusions (includes finding a relationship among seemingly unrelated events).

label: Information Ordering
entry_text: The ability to arrange things or actions in a certain order or pattern according to a specific rule or set of rules (e.g., patterns of numbers, letters, words, pictures, mathematical operations).

label: Ingenuity
entry_text: Ingenuity is the capacity to devise a resourceful solution when standard methods or available resources are insufficient.
example: A teacher turns spare cardboard and rubber bands into a working model of a lever for class.

label: Manual Dexterity
entry_text: The ability to quickly move your hand, your hand together with your arm, or your two hands to grasp, manipulate, or assemble objects.

label: Mathematical Reasoning
entry_text: The ability to choose the right mathematical methods or formulas to solve a problem.

label: Memorization
entry_text: The ability to remember information such as words, numbers, pictures, and procedures.

label: Multilimb Coordination
entry_text: The ability to coordinate two or more limbs (for example, two arms, two legs, or one leg and one arm) while sitting, standing, or lying down. It does not involve performing the activities while the whole body is in motion.

label: Near Vision
entry_text: The ability to see details at close range (within a few feet of the observer).

label: Night Vision
entry_text: The ability to see under low-light conditions.

label: Number Facility
entry_text: The ability to add, subtract, multiply, or divide quickly and correctly.

label: Oral Comprehension
entry_text: The ability to listen to and understand information and ideas presented through spoken words and sentences.

label: Oral Expression
entry_text: The ability to communicate information and ideas in speaking so others will understand.

label: Originality
entry_text: The ability to come up with unusual or clever ideas about a given topic or situation, or to develop creative ways to solve a problem.

label: Patience
entry_text: Patience is the capacity to tolerate delay, repetition, or frustration while continuing to act deliberately.
example: A mentor lets a learner work through several attempts before offering another hint.

label: Perceptual Speed
entry_text: The ability to quickly and accurately compare similarities and differences among sets of letters, numbers, objects, pictures, or patterns. The things to be compared may be presented at the same time or one after the other. This ability also includes comparing a presented object with a remembered object.

label: Peripheral Vision
entry_text: The ability to see objects or movement of objects to one's side when the eyes are looking ahead.

label: Problem Sensitivity
entry_text: The ability to tell when something is wrong or is likely to go wrong. It does not involve solving the problem, only recognizing that there is a problem.

label: Quick learning
entry_text: Quick learning is the capacity to acquire and apply unfamiliar information or procedures with relatively little instruction or practice.
example: After a short demonstration, a technician correctly uses an unfamiliar inventory screen to receive a shipment.

label: Rate Control
entry_text: The ability to time your movements or the movement of a piece of equipment in anticipation of changes in the speed and/or direction of a moving object or scene.

label: Reaction Time
entry_text: The ability to quickly respond (with the hand, finger, or foot) to a signal (sound, light, picture) when it appears.

label: Resilience
entry_text: Resilience is the capacity to recover or adapt after setbacks, adversity, or sustained pressure.
example: After a prototype fails a trial, a team member processes the feedback and returns to the work with a revised plan.

label: Response Orientation
entry_text: The ability to choose quickly between two or more movements in response to two or more different signals (lights, sounds, pictures). It includes the speed with which the correct response is started with the hand, foot, or other body part.

label: Results-oriented
entry_text: Being results-oriented is a tendency to judge work by its demonstrated outcomes rather than by activity alone.
example: A support lead checks whether a new help page reduced repeat questions, not just how many articles were published.
sense_note: The adjectival label describes a work orientation.

label: Selective Attention
entry_text: The ability to concentrate on a task over a period of time without being distracted.

label: Self-confidence
entry_text: Self-confidence is trust in one's capacity to act or exercise judgment in a situation, without implying that the judgment is correct.
example: A junior designer explains a design choice to a review panel while remaining open to counterevidence.
sense_note: Better understood as a disposition or belief than as a discrete cognitive ability.

label: Self-starter
entry_text: A self-starter identifies and begins useful work without needing detailed instructions or repeated prompting.
example: A new coordinator notices unanswered inquiries and creates a queue to track and route them.
sense_note: The label names a person characterized by initiative.

label: Sound Localization
entry_text: The ability to tell the direction from which a sound originated.

label: Spatial Orientation
entry_text: The ability to know your location in relation to the environment or to know where other objects are in relation to you.

label: Spatial-temporal reasoning
entry_text: Spatial-temporal reasoning is the ability to infer how positions, shapes, or spatial relationships change over time.
example: A player predicts where a bouncing ball will reach the edge of the court after it strikes a wall.

label: Speech Clarity
entry_text: The ability to speak clearly so others can understand you.

label: Speech Recognition
entry_text: The ability to identify and understand the speech of another person.

label: Speed of Closure
entry_text: The ability to quickly make sense of, combine, and organize information into meaningful patterns.

label: Speed of Limb Movement
entry_text: The ability to quickly move the arms and legs.

label: Stamina
entry_text: The ability to exert yourself physically over long periods of time without getting winded or out of breath.

label: Static Strength
entry_text: The ability to exert maximum muscle force to lift, push, pull, or carry objects.

label: Success-driven
entry_text: Being success-driven is a tendency to seek achievement and persist in pursuit of a high standard of performance.
example: After falling short of a benchmark, a runner adjusts training and works toward a measurable improvement.
sense_note: The label describes motivation rather than a discrete ability.

label: Team-oriented
entry_text: Being team-oriented is a tendency to coordinate one's contributions with others in support of shared goals.
example: An engineer documents a handoff early so the next team can continue without waiting for a meeting.
sense_note: The adjectival label describes a work orientation.

label: Time Sharing
entry_text: The ability to shift back and forth between two or more activities or sources of information (such as speech, sounds, touch, or other sources).

label: Trunk Strength
entry_text: The ability to use your abdominal and lower back muscles to support part of the body repeatedly or continuously over time without "giving out" or fatiguing.

label: Visual Color Discrimination
entry_text: The ability to match or detect differences between colors, including shades of color and brightness.

label: Visualization
entry_text: The ability to imagine how something will look after it is moved around or when its parts are moved or rearranged.

label: Wrist-Finger Speed
entry_text: The ability to make fast, simple, repeated movements of the fingers, hands, and wrists.

label: Written Comprehension
entry_text: The ability to read and understand information and ideas presented in writing.

label: Written Expression
entry_text: The ability to communicate information and ideas in writing so others will understand.

label: 3D Touch
entry_text: 3D Touch is Apple's pressure-sensitive touchscreen feature that lets a supported device respond differently to touches of different force.
example: A user presses firmly on a supported iPhone app icon to reveal a shortcut menu.

label: ABEC scale
entry_text: The ABEC scale classifies certain precision bearings by dimensional and running tolerances, not by overall durability or suitability for a particular use.
example: A machine designer specifies an ABEC tolerance class for a spindle bearing rather than inferring its load rating from that class.

label: Access point name
entry_text: An access point name, or APN, identifies the packet data network a mobile device requests from its carrier.
example: A technician selects a carrier's enterprise APN to connect a compatible device to the organization's designated data network.

label: Accumulated benefit obligation
entry_text: An accumulated benefit obligation is the actuarial present value of defined pension benefits earned to date, based on current rather than projected future compensation.
example: A pension actuary estimates obligations for service already performed without assuming future salary increases.

label: Action for Climate Empowerment
entry_text: Action for Climate Empowerment is the UN climate framework for strengthening education, training, public awareness, participation, public access to information, and international cooperation on climate change.
example: A national program combines teacher training and public consultations so people can participate in developing climate policy.

label: Active pharmaceutical ingredient
entry_text: An active pharmaceutical ingredient is a substance in a medicine intended to produce its pharmacological activity or another direct effect relevant to its intended use.
example: Acetaminophen is the active ingredient in a tablet whose other ingredients help hold the tablet together.

label: Activities of daily living
entry_text: Activities of daily living are basic personal self-care tasks such as bathing, dressing, eating, and using the toilet.
example: A clinician assesses whether a person can dress without assistance when planning a safe return home.

label: Actuarial exams
entry_text: Actuarial exams are professional assessments of quantitative and business knowledge required along actuarial credentialing pathways.
example: An aspiring actuary takes a probability exam as one step toward professional qualification.
sense_note: The label names examinations, not a field of knowledge.

label: Administration and Management
entry_text: Knowledge of business and management principles involved in strategic planning, resource allocation, human resources modeling, leadership technique, production methods, and coordination of people and resources.

label: Administrative
entry_text: Knowledge of administrative and office procedures and systems such as word processing, managing files and records, stenography and transcription, designing forms, and workplace terminology.

label: Administrative law
entry_text: Administrative law governs the authority, procedures, decisions, and legal review of government administrative bodies.
example: A lawyer checks whether a licensing agency provided the required hearing before revoking a license.

label: Advanced Automatic Collision Notification
entry_text: Advanced Automatic Collision Notification uses vehicle crash sensors and telematics to transmit crash information for emergency response and may estimate injury risk from the transmitted data.
example: A response center receives the location and severity indicators after a crash even though the occupants cannot call for help.

label: Airworthiness engineering
entry_text: Airworthiness engineering establishes and demonstrates that an aircraft or aircraft system meets applicable safety requirements for flight and continued operation.
example: An engineering team documents and tests whether a redesigned landing gear meets certification loads.

label: Analogue electronics
entry_text: Analogue electronics is the study and design of circuits that process continuously varying electrical signals.
example: An engineer designs an amplifier to raise a microphone's small voltage signal to a usable level.

label: Ancient history
entry_text: Ancient history studies societies and events of the ancient past through evidence such as texts, inscriptions, artifacts, and material remains.
example: A historian compares trade records with recovered ceramics to reconstruct relationships between ancient port cities.

label: Ancient philosophy
entry_text: Ancient philosophy studies philosophical arguments and traditions developed in ancient societies, including accounts of knowledge, reality, and how to live.
example: A class compares Stoic and Epicurean arguments about what makes a life good.

label: Andragogy
entry_text: Andragogy is the study and practice of helping adults learn, especially through instruction that draws on their experience and addresses practical goals.
example: An instructor asks working nurses to use their own handoff cases in a course on communication.

label: Animal science
entry_text: Animal science studies the biology, nutrition, breeding, behavior, and care of animals, especially domesticated species.
example: A researcher compares feeding programs for their effects on the growth and health of dairy calves.

label: Anthropometrics
entry_text: Anthropometrics is the measurement and analysis of human body dimensions and their variation across individuals and populations.
example: A designer uses distributions of forearm length and seated reach to position a height-adjustable control panel.

label: Anti-bribery and corruption
entry_text: Anti-bribery and corruption encompasses the rules and controls used to prevent, identify, and respond to improper inducements and abuses of entrusted power.
example: A procurement team has a prospective supplier's gifts reviewed for conflicts before contract negotiations.

label: Application controls
entry_text: Application controls are checks within an information system that protect the validity, completeness, and accuracy of the transactions it processes.
example: An accounts-payable application rejects an invoice that duplicates a supplier and invoice-number combination already entered.

label: Application delivery network
entry_text: An application delivery network is a set of network services that distributes, accelerates, and protects access to applications.
example: An application delivery network sends users to healthy application instances and protects the public entry point from abusive traffic.

label: Application pool
entry_text: An application pool groups web applications under shared worker-process settings and isolates their execution from applications in separate pools.
example: An IIS administrator places a billing site in its own application pool so recycling its worker does not restart the document portal.
sense_note: The usual sense is Microsoft's IIS hosting concept.

label: Application programming interface
entry_text: An application programming interface defines the operations, inputs, and outputs through which software components interact.
example: A scheduling app requests available appointment times from a clinic system through its API.

label: Application-specific integrated circuit
entry_text: An application-specific integrated circuit is a chip designed to perform a particular application rather than general-purpose computation.
example: A network appliance uses a chip designed specifically to forward packets at high throughput.

label: Applied linguistics
entry_text: Applied linguistics uses research on language to address practical problems such as language teaching, assessment, and communication.
example: A researcher tests whether a redesigned proficiency test better reflects the language tasks students perform in class.

label: Applied statistics
entry_text: Applied statistics uses statistical methods to design studies and draw evidence-based conclusions from data in practical settings.
example: An analyst estimates delivery-time variability from sample routes to recommend a realistic service window.

label: Archaeology
entry_text: Archaeology reconstructs and interprets past human activity by studying artifacts, structures, sites, and other material traces in context.
example: An archaeologist compares the remains in successive soil layers to infer how a settlement's food practices changed.

label: Arithmetic
entry_text: Arithmetic concerns basic numerical operations and the relationships among them, such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
example: A cook multiplies each ingredient quantity by three to prepare enough portions for a larger group.

label: ARP4754
entry_text: ARP4754 is an SAE aerospace recommended practice for developing civil aircraft and systems using structured requirements, validation, verification, and development assurance.
example: An avionics program uses the guidance to trace a system safety requirement through allocation and verification.
sense_note: Specific revisions have different designations; the label does not specify one.

label: Art education
entry_text: Art education studies and practices teaching people to create, interpret, and evaluate visual and other artistic work.
example: A teacher has students compare how changing composition alters the focus of their photographs.

label: Art history
entry_text: Art history studies works of art in relation to their dates, places, materials, makers, patrons, audiences, and historical contexts.
example: An art historian compares altar paintings and commissioning records to understand what a church expected a painting to communicate.

label: Art theory
entry_text: Art theory investigates the concepts and arguments used to define, interpret, and evaluate art and artistic practice.
example: A critic uses theories of institutional recognition to explain why displaying a common object in a gallery may change how it is understood.

label: Arterial blood gas testing
entry_text: Arterial blood gas testing measures properties such as blood pH and oxygen and carbon dioxide partial pressures in an arterial sample to assess respiratory and acid-base status.
example: A clinician reviews the test after a change in ventilation to assess carbon dioxide clearance.

label: Artificial intelligence
entry_text: Artificial intelligence is the field concerned with building computational systems that perform tasks such as perception, reasoning, learning, or planning.
example: A game uses a search algorithm to choose a route through a maze, without needing to learn the route from examples.

label: Artificial intelligence risk
entry_text: Artificial intelligence risk concerns potential harms from the design, deployment, use, or misuse of AI systems and the conditions that make those harms more or less likely.
example: A lender evaluates whether a model could systematically misclassify applicants from a group poorly represented in its training data.

label: ASC 340
entry_text: ASC 340 is the U.S. accounting codification topic Other Assets and Deferred Costs, whose subtopics address accounting for specified assets or costs, including certain contract costs.
example: An accountant consults its contract-cost guidance to decide whether an incremental sales commission should be capitalized.

label: Asset turnover
entry_text: Asset turnover is a ratio that measures how much net sales a business generates per unit of average assets during a period.
example: A retailer with $6 million in annual net sales and $3 million in average assets reports asset turnover of 2.

label: Athletic training
entry_text: Athletic training is a health profession focused on preventing, evaluating, managing, and rehabilitating injuries and conditions associated with physical activity.
example: An athletic trainer assesses an athlete's ankle injury and coordinates a staged return to participation.
sense_note: Distinguish the health profession from athletic performance conditioning.

label: Attorney-client privilege
entry_text: Attorney-client privilege is a legal protection against compelled disclosure of qualifying confidential communications between a lawyer and a client for the purpose of obtaining or giving legal advice.
example: An organization claims privilege over a confidential email to its lawyer requesting advice about a contract dispute.
sense_note: Scope and exceptions vary by jurisdiction; not all attorney communications are privileged.

label: Authorised capital
entry_text: Authorised capital is the maximum amount of share capital a company is permitted to issue under its governing documents or applicable legal framework.
example: A company checks its authorised capital before issuing new shares to investors.
sense_note: Terms and requirements vary by jurisdiction.

label: Automated information systems security
entry_text: Automated information systems security protects computer-based information systems and their data against unauthorized access, alteration, or disruption.
example: An organization limits access by job role and verifies its backups so users can recover records after a system failure.

label: Automotive finance
entry_text: Automotive finance concerns the structures, costs, and risks of loans, leases, and other arrangements that fund vehicles or vehicle inventories.
example: A dealership compares the financing costs of carrying unsold vehicles under different inventory-credit terms.

label: Automotive loans
entry_text: An automotive loan is credit used to purchase a vehicle, which typically serves as collateral for repayment.
example: A borrower compares monthly payments and total interest for the same car under two loan terms.

label: Autonomic nervous system
entry_text: The autonomic nervous system regulates functions typically outside conscious control, including heart rate, digestion, and blood vessel tone.
example: When someone stands, autonomic reflexes can help maintain blood pressure by adjusting heart rate and vascular tone.

label: B-tree
entry_text: A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree that keeps keys sorted and limits the number of nodes visited for lookups and updates.
example: A database uses a B-tree index to find a range of invoice dates without scanning every invoice.

label: Bacteriology
entry_text: Bacteriology is the study of bacteria, including their diversity, structure, physiology, ecology, and roles in health and disease.
example: An instructor compares beneficial gut bacteria and disease-associated bacteria to explain why bacteria are not all harmful.

label: Barcode systems
entry_text: Barcode systems encode identifiers in machine-readable patterns and use scanners and software to connect those identifiers to records or transactions.
example: A warehouse scans a carton barcode to match the carton to its shipment record.

label: Bariatric surgery
entry_text: Bariatric surgery encompasses operations that alter the digestive system to treat obesity and associated metabolic conditions.
example: A care team compares the expected benefits and long-term follow-up needs of different bariatric operations.

label: Basic block
entry_text: A basic block is a maximal sequence of machine or intermediate instructions entered at the beginning and executed in order until control leaves at the end.
example: A compiler treats the instructions between a branch target and a conditional jump as a unit during optimization.

label: Battery technology
entry_text: Battery technology concerns devices that store chemical energy and deliver it as electrical energy, including their materials, design, safety, and performance.
example: An engineer compares cycle life and capacity when selecting batteries for a solar backup system.

label: Behavioural science
entry_text: Behavioural science examines how people or other organisms act and how psychological, social, and environmental factors shape those actions.
example: A researcher tests whether changing the default meeting reminder increases attendance.

label: Big O notation
entry_text: Big O notation describes an asymptotic upper bound on how a function grows, ignoring constant factors beyond a sufficiently large input size.
example: An algorithm using a number of comparisons proportional to the square of its input size can be described as O(n²).

label: Bill of materials
entry_text: A bill of materials lists the components, materials, quantities, and often subassemblies needed to make a product.
example: A manufacturer uses the bill of materials for a lamp to order the right numbers of housings, switches, and fasteners.

label: Binary options
entry_text: A binary option is a financial contract whose payoff takes one of two predetermined values depending on whether a specified condition holds at expiry.
example: A contract pays a fixed amount if an index is above its strike at expiry and nothing if it is not.

label: Biochemical genetics
entry_text: Biochemical genetics studies how variation in genes affects enzymes, metabolites, and other biochemical processes.
example: A researcher studies how an inherited enzyme deficiency changes levels of a metabolite in patients.

label: Biological applications of bifurcation theory
entry_text: Biological applications of bifurcation theory study how a change in a model parameter can cause a qualitative shift in the modeled behavior of a biological system.
example: An ecologist models how an increase in nutrient input might shift a lake from one persistent ecosystem state to another.

label: Biology
entry_text: Knowledge of plant and animal organisms, their tissues, cells, functions, interdependencies, and interactions with each other and the environment.

label: Biomedical informatics
entry_text: Biomedical informatics develops and applies methods for representing, managing, and using data and information in biology, medicine, and public health.
example: A hospital standardizes laboratory records so clinicians can compare a patient's results over time across departments.

label: Biomolecular engineering
entry_text: Biomolecular engineering applies engineering principles to the design, analysis, or use of biological molecules and molecular systems.
example: A materials team studies how molecular properties affect the performance of a protein-based material.

label: Biopesticide
entry_text: A biopesticide is a pest-control agent based on a living organism, a naturally derived substance, or a pesticidal substance produced by a plant, subject to how the term is defined by the regulator.
example: A grower checks whether a registered insect-control product is classified as a biopesticide.

label: Biosensors
entry_text: Biosensors combine a biological recognition element with a signal-converting component to detect or measure a substance or condition.
example: A glucose meter converts a reaction involving glucose into an electrical signal used to estimate its concentration.

label: Bioterrorism preparedness and response
entry_text: Bioterrorism preparedness and response encompasses public-health planning, detection, communication, and coordinated care to limit harm from deliberate biological incidents.
example: A public-health team runs a tabletop exercise to check how hospitals and health agencies would coordinate public information.

label: Bismuth sulfite agar
entry_text: Bismuth sulfite agar is a selective and differential microbiological medium historically used in screening for certain Salmonella, including Salmonella Typhi.
example: A microbiology student identifies the medium in an archival laboratory report and distinguishes a presumptive screen from confirmation.

label: Boiler draft
entry_text: Boiler draft is the pressure difference that moves combustion air into a boiler and carries flue gases out.
example: A plant operator monitors draft to distinguish restricted flue flow from normal boiler operation.

label: Boolean algebra
entry_text: Boolean algebra is a formal system for combining and simplifying true-or-false values using operations such as AND, OR, and NOT.
example: A designer uses Boolean algebra to simplify the logic determining whether a warning light turns on.

label: Border studies
entry_text: Border studies examines how territorial boundaries are created, governed, crossed, and experienced and how they shape communities and identities.
example: A researcher studies how new border procedures change the daily commute of workers in neighboring towns.

label: Breast surgery
entry_text: Breast surgery encompasses operations on breast tissue performed for diagnosis, treatment, reconstruction, or changes in appearance.
example: A surgical team plans how breast reconstruction might fit into a patient's treatment and recovery schedule.

label: Builder's risk insurance
entry_text: Builder's risk insurance covers specified property loss or damage to a building under construction and may cover related materials, subject to policy terms.
example: After a covered fire damages an unfinished building, the project owner consults the policy to determine whether replacement materials qualify.

label: Building and Construction
entry_text: Knowledge of materials, methods, and the tools involved in the construction or repair of houses, buildings, or other structures such as highways and roads.

label: Callback function
entry_text: A callback is a function supplied to another component so that component can invoke it at a designated point or in response to an event.
example: A program gives its file reader a callback that updates the screen once reading finishes.

label: Cannabis regulations
entry_text: Cannabis regulations are jurisdiction-specific rules governing permitted activities involving cannabis, such as production, testing, sale, possession, and use.
example: A compliance worker checks labeling and testing requirements before releasing a regulated product in a particular jurisdiction.

label: Capital asset pricing model
entry_text: The capital asset pricing model relates an asset's expected return to the risk-free rate and its sensitivity to the market risk premium.
example: An analyst uses a firm's equity beta and an assumed market premium to estimate its cost of equity.

label: Captive insurance
entry_text: Captive insurance uses an insurer owned or controlled by the organization or group it is formed to insure.
example: Several affiliated companies use a captive insurer to pool a defined share of their own property risks.

label: Cardiac surgery
entry_text: Cardiac surgery is the surgical treatment of conditions affecting the heart and its closely associated major vessels.
example: A surgical team repairs a damaged heart valve to restore more effective blood flow.

label: Cardiothoracic surgery
entry_text: Cardiothoracic surgery is the specialty concerned with operations on the heart and other organs and structures of the chest.
example: A cardiothoracic service includes both heart valve procedures and operations to remove diseased lung tissue.

label: Cardiovascular physiology
entry_text: Cardiovascular physiology studies how the heart, blood vessels, and their regulatory mechanisms circulate blood and maintain tissue perfusion.
example: A student explains how heart rate and stroke volume contribute to increased cardiac output during exercise.

label: Chemical reactions
entry_text: Chemical reactions transform substances by rearranging atoms, ions, or electrons to form products with chemical identities different from the reactants.
example: Iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of moisture to form products commonly called rust.

label: Chemistry
entry_text: Knowledge of the chemical composition, structure, and properties of substances and of the chemical processes and transformations that they undergo. This includes uses of chemicals and their interactions, danger signs, production techniques, and disposal methods.

label: Child and adolescent psychiatry
entry_text: Child and adolescent psychiatry is the medical specialty concerned with assessing, preventing, and treating mental health conditions in children and adolescents.
example: A psychiatrist works with a teenager, family, and school to assess how anxiety affects attendance.

label: Child nutrition
entry_text: Child nutrition concerns children's dietary needs, feeding practices, and the relationship between nutrients, growth, development, and health.
example: A school meal planner considers age-appropriate portions and nutrient needs when designing a lunch menu.

label: Children's Health Insurance Program
entry_text: The Children's Health Insurance Program is a U.S. federal-state program that provides coverage to eligible children, generally in families whose income is too high for Medicaid but insufficient for affordable private coverage.
example: A family checks its state's CHIP eligibility after learning its children do not qualify for Medicaid.

label: Children's ministry
entry_text: Children's ministry is the work of a religious community to provide children with age-appropriate religious education, participation, and pastoral care.
example: A congregation organizes a supervised children's lesson using stories, questions, and activities suited to different ages.

label: Chlorofluorocarbons
entry_text: Chlorofluorocarbons are compounds containing carbon, chlorine, and fluorine that can deplete stratospheric ozone after breaking down and releasing chlorine.
example: A technician identifies a legacy refrigerant as a CFC when documenting equipment for proper disposal.

label: Choral music
entry_text: Choral music is music composed or arranged for a group of singers, who may sing in unison or in multiple parts.
example: A choir rehearses a piece in which sopranos and altos sing different melodic lines against the tenors and basses.

label: Circular economy
entry_text: A circular economy aims to reduce waste and demand for new resources by keeping products, components, and materials in use through design, reuse, repair, remanufacturing, or recycling.
example: An appliance company replaces worn components in returned machines and sells the refurbished units instead of scrapping them.

label: Circulatory system
entry_text: The circulatory system is the heart, blood, and blood vessels working together to distribute oxygen and nutrients and carry wastes away from tissues.
example: Blood travels from the heart to the lungs to take up oxygen before returning to be pumped through the body.

label: Client access license
entry_text: A client access license grants a specified user or device the right to access licensed server software under a vendor's terms.
example: An organization compares per-user and per-device licenses for staff who share workstations.

label: Climate variability and change
entry_text: Climate variability and change concern fluctuations around expected climate conditions and persistent shifts in their distributions over longer periods, respectively.
example: A climatologist distinguishes a cluster of unusually dry years from a multidecade shift in rainfall.

label: Clinical informatics
entry_text: Clinical informatics applies information science and computing to improve clinical workflows, patient care, and the use of health data.
example: A clinical informatics team redesigns medication alerts so high-priority safety warnings reach the prescribing clinician.

label: Clinical medical ethics
entry_text: Clinical medical ethics applies ethical principles to decisions and relationships arising in patient care.
example: An ethics consultant helps a care team assess how to honor an incapacitated patient's previously expressed wishes.

label: Clinical pastoral education
entry_text: Clinical pastoral education trains spiritual care providers through supervised practice, reflection, and feedback in clinical or other care settings.
example: A chaplain trainee reviews a conversation with a patient alongside a supervisor to understand what support the patient wanted.

label: Cloud computing
entry_text: Cloud computing delivers on-demand computing resources over a network from a shared pool that can be provisioned and released as needed.
example: A research group rents temporary computing capacity for a data analysis instead of buying a server.

label: Cloud computing security
entry_text: Cloud computing security protects data, applications, identities, and infrastructure in cloud environments according to the responsibilities of providers and customers.
example: An organization restricts access to a cloud storage bucket and audits which identities may read its records.

label: Coastal engineering
entry_text: Coastal engineering studies and designs interventions for waves, currents, sediment transport, erosion, and flooding along shores.
example: An engineer models how a proposed breakwater might change beach erosion and harbor wave conditions.

label: Cognitive computing
entry_text: Cognitive computing is a broad label for computer systems designed to support or approximate human capabilities such as interpreting language, recognizing patterns, and reasoning from evidence.
example: A system highlights relevant passages from documents for a reviewer answering a question.
sense_note: The label is used inconsistently and does not imply consciousness or a single technical architecture.

label: Cognitive load
entry_text: Cognitive load is the mental effort a task places on limited working-memory resources.
example: A teacher puts diagram labels next to the parts they name so students do not have to remember a separate key.

label: Color rendering index
entry_text: The color rendering index rates how faithfully a light source renders specified sample colors relative to a reference illuminant under a standardized method.
example: A museum compares lamp CRI ratings before testing how textiles actually look under each light.

label: Commercial off-the-shelf
entry_text: Commercial off-the-shelf products are commercially available in standard form and used without being developed specifically for a particular buyer.
example: A lab purchases an existing meter from a vendor's catalog rather than commissioning a custom instrument.

label: Commons-based peer production
entry_text: Commons-based peer production is distributed collaboration in which participants contribute to a shared resource under rules that permit collective use or improvement.
example: Volunteers maintain an openly licensed encyclopedia by writing, reviewing, and revising one another's entries.

label: Communication theories
entry_text: Communication theories explain how people or systems create, transmit, interpret, and respond to messages in different contexts.
example: A researcher applies framing theory to examine how two headlines lead readers to interpret the same event differently.

label: Communications and Media
entry_text: Knowledge of media production, communication, and dissemination techniques and methods. This includes alternative ways to inform and entertain via written, oral, and visual media.

label: Community nutrition
entry_text: Community nutrition addresses the food access, dietary patterns, and nutritional health of populations through assessment, education, and local interventions.
example: A public health department uses neighborhood survey data to decide where to open a subsidized produce market.

label: Community resilience
entry_text: Community resilience is the capacity of a community to maintain essential functions, adapt, and recover when exposed to disturbances or sustained stress.
example: A neighborhood organizes transportation and communications so residents can reach cooling centers during a power outage.

label: Computer architecture
entry_text: Computer architecture concerns how processors, memory, input and output, and their interfaces are organized to execute programs.
example: A designer weighs cache size and memory latency when comparing processor designs for a data-intensive workload.

label: Computer networking
entry_text: Computer networking concerns connecting devices and coordinating how they address, transmit, route, and receive data.
example: A network engineer configures office devices to exchange data across two buildings through a routed connection.

label: Computer science
entry_text: Computer science studies computation, including algorithms, data representation, programming languages, software, and the systems that execute them.
example: A researcher compares algorithms for finding the shortest route through a large graph.

label: Computers and Electronics
entry_text: Knowledge of circuit boards, processors, chips, electronic equipment, and computer hardware and software, including applications and programming.

label: Control loops
entry_text: A control loop measures a system's behavior and feeds the result back to a controller that adjusts an input toward a desired condition.
example: A thermostat senses room temperature and turns heating on when the temperature falls below the set threshold.

label: Control valves and flow characteristics
entry_text: Control valves adjust fluid flow, and their flow characteristics describe how flow capacity changes with valve travel under specified conditions.
example: An engineer compares linear and equal-percentage valve characteristics before selecting a valve for a varying demand range.

label: Conversational AI
entry_text: Conversational AI comprises systems that use written or spoken dialogue to interpret input and generate responses or take actions.
example: A service bot asks a caller for an appointment date and then confirms which available slot they want.

label: Convolutional neural networks
entry_text: Convolutional neural networks use learned filters with shared weights across local regions to process spatially or sequentially structured data.
example: An image classifier learns filters that respond to edges in different parts of a photograph.

label: Corporate finance
entry_text: Corporate finance concerns how firms invest, raise funds, manage financial risk, and allocate returns to owners.
example: A company compares the expected cash flows of two expansion projects before deciding where to invest.

label: Correspondent banking
entry_text: Correspondent banking is an arrangement in which one bank provides services such as payments or account access to another bank.
example: A smaller bank sends an international payment through a correspondent with access to the receiving currency's payment system.

label: Cosmetic dermatology
entry_text: Cosmetic dermatology addresses the appearance of skin and related structures using dermatologic evaluation and treatments.
example: A dermatologist evaluates whether a patient's uneven skin pigmentation is a suitable concern for cosmetic treatment.

label: Cost accounting
entry_text: Cost accounting identifies, assigns, and analyzes costs to understand the resources consumed by products, services, processes, or operations.
example: A manufacturer estimates production cost per unit by combining materials, labor, and allocated factory overhead.

label: Counterparty risk
entry_text: Counterparty risk is the possibility of loss if another party fails to perform its obligations under a financial transaction or contract.
example: A bank reviews whether another institution could fail to make required payments under a currency swap.

label: Craniofacial surgery
entry_text: Craniofacial surgery treats congenital, acquired, or traumatic conditions involving the skull and facial structures.
example: A multidisciplinary team plans a staged reconstruction for a child with a congenital skull and facial difference.

label: Criminal intelligence
entry_text: Criminal intelligence is systematically collected and analyzed information used to understand suspected criminal activity and inform lawful prevention or investigation.
example: Analysts look for patterns in reported incidents and document uncertainty before sharing an assessment with investigators.

label: Crop farming
entry_text: Crop farming is the cultivation of plants for food, fiber, feed, or other products, including planning, planting, care, and harvest.
example: A grower rotates legumes with grain crops to help manage soil fertility and pest pressure.

label: Cross-domain solutions
entry_text: Cross-domain solutions control authorized information access or transfer between security domains with different trust levels or policies.
example: An agency uses an approved gateway to review what information may be shared between separately protected networks.
sense_note: Interpreted as the information-security term; outside that context the phrase can mean any solution spanning disciplines.

label: Cross product
entry_text: The cross product of two vectors in three-dimensional Euclidean space is a vector perpendicular to both, oriented by the right-hand rule and with magnitude equal to the area they span.
example: A graphics program takes the cross product of two triangle edges to calculate a surface normal.
sense_note: Interpreted as the vector operation; some fields use the phrase informally for a Cartesian product.

label: CRUD
entry_text: CRUD stands for create, read, update, and delete, the four basic operations for managing stored records.
example: A contact manager lets users add, view, edit, or remove a contact.

label: Cryptocurrency
entry_text: A cryptocurrency is a digitally represented asset whose transfers or issuance are secured by cryptography, usually through a distributed ledger.
example: A wallet signs a transfer request that the associated network can validate against its ledger.

label: Custom post types
entry_text: Custom post types are developer-defined WordPress content categories with their own names and configured editing, display, or routing behavior.
example: A museum stores its exhibitions as a distinct post type instead of mixing them into blog posts.
sense_note: The phrase is specifically associated with WordPress; a post type is not the same as a taxonomy term.

label: Customer and Personal Service
entry_text: Knowledge of principles and processes for providing customer and personal services. This includes customer needs assessment, meeting quality standards for services, and evaluation of customer satisfaction.

label: Cyber resilience
entry_text: Cyber resilience is the capacity to maintain or restore essential digital functions when cyber incidents disrupt systems despite preventive controls.
example: An organization rehearses restoring its records and switching to a fallback process after simulated downtime.

label: Cybersecurity
entry_text: Cybersecurity is the protection of computer systems, networks, and data against unauthorized access, misuse, damage, or disruption.
example: A university combines access controls, security monitoring, and incident response procedures to protect student records.

label: Dairy science
entry_text: Dairy science studies milk production, composition, quality, and processing into products such as cheese, yogurt, and butter.
example: A dairy scientist measures how storage conditions affect the quality of milk sent to a processor.

label: Data as a Service
entry_text: Data as a Service delivers datasets to consumers through a managed network interface or feed rather than requiring each consumer to collect and maintain the data.
example: A transit dashboard retrieves a provider's regularly updated ridership data through a subscription interface.

label: Data localization
entry_text: Data localization is a requirement to store, process, or retain specified data within a designated jurisdiction, depending on the applicable rule.
example: A company checks whether a rule requiring an in-country copy of certain records still allows a backup abroad.
sense_note: Localization requirements vary and are not synonymous with choosing where data resides.

label: Data storage technologies
entry_text: Data storage technologies are the media, devices, and systems used to retain and retrieve digital information.
example: An archive chooses tape for infrequently accessed backups and solid-state storage for frequently consulted catalogs.

label: Database as a service
entry_text: Database as a service provides a remotely hosted database whose provider manages infrastructure and agreed operational tasks such as backups, patching, or replication.
example: An application team provisions a managed PostgreSQL database instead of maintaining its own database server.

label: Database life cycle
entry_text: The database life cycle covers planning, designing, implementing, operating, evolving, and eventually retiring or replacing a database.
example: A team migrates an active membership database to a revised schema while preserving its records and validating the change.

label: Database systems
entry_text: Database systems combine organized collections of data with software that manages access, queries, changes, integrity, and recovery.
example: An inventory system records a shipment and updates available stock in a single transaction.

label: Database trigger
entry_text: A database trigger runs a defined action automatically when a specified event occurs in the database.
example: An update trigger records a time and table name in an audit log when a protected record changes.

label: Debits and credits
entry_text: Debits and credits are the left- and right-side entries of double-entry accounting, and their effects on balances depend on the account type.
example: A cash purchase of supplies debits the supplies asset account and credits the cash asset account.

label: Deposition (geology)
entry_text: Deposition is the geological process by which transported material settles or accumulates when water, wind, ice, or gravity no longer carries it onward.
example: A river deposits sediment as its flow slows entering a lake.

label: Design
entry_text: Knowledge of design techniques, tools, and principles involved in production of precision technical plans, blueprints, drawings, and models.

label: Diagnostic audiology
entry_text: Diagnostic audiology uses tests of hearing and auditory function to characterize hearing differences and help determine their nature or possible source.
example: An audiologist compares air- and bone-conduction thresholds to investigate whether sound conduction is contributing to a hearing loss.

label: Dialectology
entry_text: Dialectology studies systematic variation in language across regional or social groups, drawing on features such as pronunciation, grammar, and vocabulary.
example: A researcher maps where speakers use different words for the same household object without ranking one variety above another.

label: Dietetics
entry_text: Dietetics applies food and nutrition science to assess dietary needs and develop strategies that support health or manage disease.
example: A dietitian adapts a meal plan to a patient's reported food preferences, available foods, and prescribed nutrient needs.

label: Digital currencies
entry_text: Digital currencies are monetary units represented and transferred electronically, including forms that do not rely on cryptocurrency networks.
example: A central bank pilots a digital form of its currency for electronic retail payments.

label: Digital health technologies
entry_text: Digital health technologies use software, electronics, or communications to support health, care delivery, or health-system operations.
example: A clinic uses a remote monitoring platform to review blood pressure readings patients send from home.

label: Digital humanities
entry_text: Digital humanities integrates computing with humanities research and teaching to analyze, present, and interrogate cultural materials.
example: A historian maps locations mentioned in digitized letters to explore how a correspondence network changed over time.

label: Digital rights management
entry_text: Digital rights management uses technical controls and permission rules to govern access to and use of digital works.
example: A library ebook system checks that a loan is current before granting access to an encrypted book.

label: Direct digital control
entry_text: Direct digital control uses a digital controller to read process inputs, compute control decisions, and command actuators directly.
example: A building controller uses a temperature reading to update an air damper position according to a programmed control rule.

label: Disability insurance
entry_text: Disability insurance provides benefits, often partial income replacement, when a covered disability meets the policy's definition and other terms.
example: An employee checks a short-term disability policy's waiting period after an injury prevents them from working.

label: Disaster loans
entry_text: Disaster loans are repayable funds supplied under designated programs to help eligible borrowers recover from losses caused by a qualifying disaster.
example: A small business checks whether it can borrow under a disaster program to replace flood-damaged equipment.

label: Distributed computing
entry_text: Distributed computing coordinates multiple networked computers to complete related computations or provide a joint service.
example: A data processing framework assigns separate chunks of a large dataset to several machines and combines the results.

label: Documentation lifecycle
entry_text: A documentation lifecycle spans planning, authoring, reviewing, publishing, maintaining, and retiring documentation as the underlying subject changes.
example: A release owner updates the installation guide and archives instructions that apply only to an unsupported version.

label: Dot matrix printing
entry_text: Dot matrix printing uses arrays of dots to form text and graphics, usually through pins striking an inked ribbon against paper.
example: A shop prints a delivery slip and its carbon-copy duplicates on an impact dot matrix printer.
sense_note: Interpreted as the familiar impact printer technology.

label: Drug absorption
entry_text: Drug absorption is the movement of a drug from its administration site into systemic circulation.
example: A pharmacology class compares how two oral formulations differ in the rate at which the medicine appears in blood.

label: Dynamic-link library
entry_text: A dynamic-link library contains code or other resources that a program can link to or load at runtime rather than incorporating them into its own executable at build time.
example: Two Windows programs load a shared DLL to use the same image-decoding routines.
sense_note: The term DLL is especially associated with Windows; shared libraries serve similar purposes on other platforms.

label: Early childhood mental health
entry_text: Early childhood mental health concerns young children's developing capacity to experience and regulate emotions, build relationships, and explore and learn in supportive environments.
example: A clinician observes a toddler's interactions with a caregiver to understand how their relationship supports emotional regulation.

label: Earthing systems
entry_text: Earthing systems connect specified points and conductive parts of electrical installations to earth to provide a reference and help manage electrical fault and shock risks.
example: An electrical designer verifies that protective earthing works with the installation's protective devices to clear a fault.

label: Economics and Accounting
entry_text: Knowledge of economic and accounting principles and practices, the financial markets, banking, and the analysis and reporting of financial data.

label: Education and Training
entry_text: Knowledge of principles and methods for curriculum and training design, teaching and instruction for individuals and groups, and the measurement of training effects.

label: Educational assessment
entry_text: Educational assessment gathers and interprets evidence of learners' knowledge, skills, or progress to inform instruction or support decisions about achievement.
example: A teacher uses an exit question to identify which fraction concept needs reteaching before the next lesson.

label: Electrical power quality
entry_text: Electrical power quality describes how closely supply voltage, frequency, and waveforms meet conditions required for connected equipment to operate reliably.
example: An engineer checks whether brief voltage sags coincide with unexpected equipment resets.

label: Electromechanical engineering
entry_text: Electromechanical engineering designs and analyzes systems in which electrical and mechanical components exchange energy or information.
example: An engineer specifies a motor, transmission, and position sensor for a machine that moves a platform precisely.

label: Electronic article surveillance
entry_text: Electronic article surveillance uses detectable tags and sensors to help identify items leaving a monitored area without authorization.
example: A store's exit sensors alert staff when an active security tag passes through the doorway.

label: Electronic paper
entry_text: Electronic paper is a class of reflective displays designed to resemble printed paper, often retaining a static image with little or no continuous power.
example: An electronic shelf label updates its price by radio and remains readable without active illumination.

label: Emergency procedures
entry_text: Emergency procedures are predefined actions and responsibilities for protecting people, communicating, and managing an emergency until it is resolved or handed over.
example: During an evacuation drill, staff account for employees at the designated assembly point.

label: Endocannabinoid system
entry_text: The endocannabinoid system consists of endogenous signaling molecules, their receptors, and the enzymes that make and break them down, helping regulate physiological functions.
example: A physiology class examines how endocannabinoid signals can alter communication between neurons.

label: Endocrine disorders
entry_text: Endocrine disorders are conditions in which hormone production, signaling, or tissue response is impaired or excessive.
example: An endocrinologist investigates whether abnormal thyroid hormone production explains a patient's symptoms.

label: Endodontics
entry_text: Endodontics is the dental specialty concerned with the pulp and tissues surrounding the tooth root, including diagnosis and treatment of related disease or injury.
example: An endodontist evaluates an infected tooth to determine whether root canal treatment can preserve it.

label: Energy system transition
entry_text: An energy system transition is a sustained change in how energy is produced, delivered, stored, and used, including changes to infrastructure, institutions, and behavior.
example: A regional utility plans grid upgrades alongside electrified heating and more variable renewable generation.

label: Engineered materials arrestor system
entry_text: An engineered materials arrestor system is a crushable bed installed beyond a runway end to slow an aircraft that overruns the runway.
example: An airport with limited space beyond its runway installs a bed designed to deform beneath an overrunning aircraft's landing gear.

label: Engineering and Technology
entry_text: Knowledge of the practical application of engineering science and technology. This includes applying principles, techniques, procedures, and equipment to the design and production of various goods and services.

label: Engineering economics
entry_text: Engineering economics applies economic evaluation to engineering alternatives by comparing costs, benefits, timing, and uncertainty over their useful lives.
example: An engineer compares two pumps on purchase cost, energy use, maintenance, and expected replacement timing.

label: Engineering education
entry_text: Engineering education studies and practices how learners develop engineering knowledge, design judgment, technical skills, and professional responsibility.
example: An instructor evaluates student prototypes against requirements and asks teams to explain the tradeoffs behind their designs.

label: Engineering mathematics
entry_text: Engineering mathematics applies mathematical methods to modeling, analysis and design in engineering.
example: An engineer uses differential equations to predict a suspension system's motion.

label: Engineering statics
entry_text: Engineering statics studies the forces and moments on objects in equilibrium.
example: A structural engineer calculates the reactions at both supports of a beam.

label: Engineering statistics
entry_text: Engineering statistics applies probability and statistical inference to engineering data and decisions.
example: A reliability engineer estimates uncertainty in a component's average lifetime.

label: English Language
entry_text: Knowledge of the structure and content of the English language including the meaning and spelling of words, and rules of composition and grammar.

label: eNodeB
entry_text: An eNodeB is the LTE base station that manages radio communications between mobile devices and the core network.
example: An eNodeB allocates radio resources to phones in its cell.

label: Environmental anthropology
entry_text: Environmental anthropology studies how human cultures and communities interact with and understand their environments.
example: A researcher studies how fishing practices reflect local knowledge of a river.

label: Environmental finance
entry_text: Environmental finance examines how financial instruments, investment and risk management address environmental goals or impacts.
example: An analyst compares financing structures for restoring a watershed.

label: Environmental, social and governance
entry_text: Environmental, social and governance factors describe three groups of nonfinancial considerations used to evaluate organizations and investments.
example: A portfolio review considers emissions, workforce policies and board oversight.

label: Equities
entry_text: Equities are ownership interests in companies, commonly held as shares of stock.
example: A fund holds shares in several public companies as part of its equity allocation.

label: Erikson's stages of psychosocial development
entry_text: Erikson's theory divides psychosocial development into eight life stages, each organized around a characteristic conflict.
example: A developmental psychology class discusses identity versus role confusion in adolescence.

label: Ethical AI
entry_text: Ethical AI addresses how AI systems can be developed and used in ways that respect people and reduce harm.
example: A team evaluates whether an automated tool systematically disadvantages one user group.

label: Etiology
entry_text: Etiology is the origin or cause of a disease or condition, or the study of those causes.
example: An epidemiologist investigates whether several cases share the same source.

label: Excess return
entry_text: Excess return is the difference between an investment's return and a specified reference return.
example: A portfolio gaining 7 percent shows a 2-percentage-point excess return over a benchmark gaining 5 percent.
sense_note: The comparator can be a benchmark, risk-free rate or another specified reference.

label: Expectancy theory
entry_text: Expectancy theory explains motivation in terms of beliefs about whether effort leads to performance, performance to outcomes, and those outcomes are valued.
example: An employee is more willing to take on a difficult assignment when success seems attainable and the reward worthwhile.

label: Extended Parallel Process Model
entry_text: The Extended Parallel Process Model predicts responses to fear appeals from perceived threat and perceived ability to respond effectively.
example: A researcher compares whether a flood warning encourages preparation or leads recipients to tune out.

label: Extended reality
entry_text: Extended reality is an umbrella term for technologies that combine or substitute digital experiences for aspects of the physical world.
example: A training program combines augmented-reality instructions with a virtual-reality practice environment.

label: Extended validation certificate
entry_text: An extended validation certificate is a public-key certificate issued after a certificate authority performs prescribed checks on an organization's identity.
example: A company seeks extended validation to have its legal identity vetted during certificate issuance.
sense_note: Browser presentation varies; it does not establish that the site is safe.

label: Eye surgery
entry_text: Eye surgery comprises operations on the eye or its supporting structures to treat disease, injury or visual problems.
example: An ophthalmologist replaces a clouded lens during cataract surgery.

label: Factoring (finance)
entry_text: Factoring is the sale of accounts receivable to a third party, commonly to receive cash before invoices come due.
example: A distributor sells unpaid invoices to a factor rather than waiting for customer payments.

label: Family and consumer sciences
entry_text: Family and consumer sciences studies everyday decisions about resources, well-being and relationships in households and communities.
example: A class teaches families to plan a food budget around nutrition and cost.

label: Family ministry
entry_text: Family ministry is organized religious work that supports families in their relationships, spiritual life and participation in a faith community.
example: A congregation offers a parenting discussion group through its family ministry.

label: Family systems theory
entry_text: Family systems theory understands families as interdependent systems in which members' behavior and relationships influence one another.
example: A counselor examines how one person's stress changes patterns of communication across the household.

label: Feminist theory
entry_text: Feminist theory includes frameworks for examining how gendered power and inequality shape social institutions and lived experience.
example: A researcher analyzes how assumptions about caregiving shape workplace promotion practices.

label: Fibre Channel
entry_text: Fibre Channel is a high-speed networking technology used chiefly to connect servers to shared storage.
example: A data center uses Fibre Channel to connect database servers to a storage array.

label: Field-programmable gate array
entry_text: A field-programmable gate array is a chip whose digital logic circuitry can be configured after manufacture.
example: An engineer configures an FPGA to filter multiple signal channels in parallel.

label: File control block
entry_text: A file control block is a data structure that holds the metadata an operating system uses to manage a file.
example: A system consults a file control block to locate stored file data.
sense_note: The specific fields and purpose differ across operating systems.

label: Final expense insurance
entry_text: Final expense insurance is life insurance marketed to help beneficiaries cover funeral and other end-of-life costs.
example: A beneficiary uses the policy proceeds toward a funeral bill.

label: Financial privacy
entry_text: Financial privacy concerns control over who can collect, use and disclose information about a person's finances.
example: A banking app asks permission before sharing transaction history with a budgeting service.

label: Fine Arts
entry_text: Knowledge of the theory and techniques required to compose, produce, and perform works of music, dance, visual arts, drama, and sculpture.

label: Flexible Single Master Operations
entry_text: Flexible Single Master Operations are Active Directory roles that assign specific directory-wide or domain-wide operations to designated domain controllers.
example: An administrator checks which domain controller holds the schema master role before a schema change.

label: Floating-point arithmetic
entry_text: Floating-point arithmetic performs calculations on finite-precision numbers represented with a significand and exponent.
example: A programmer uses a tolerance when comparing the results of two approximate calculations.

label: Fluid statics
entry_text: Fluid statics studies pressure and forces in liquids and gases at rest.
example: An engineer calculates how water pressure increases with depth along a stationary tank wall.

label: Folk music
entry_text: Folk music includes musical traditions passed through communities and the styles that draw on those traditions.
example: Participants learn a local dance tune by playing it together at gatherings.

label: Food economics
entry_text: Food economics studies how prices, policies and incentives shape food production, distribution and consumption.
example: An economist examines how rising transport costs affect grocery prices.

label: Food microbiology
entry_text: Food microbiology studies microorganisms that affect how foods ferment, spoil or transmit illness.
example: A food scientist studies the cultures that give yogurt its texture and acidity.

label: Food process engineering
entry_text: Food process engineering applies engineering principles to design and control operations that transform or preserve foods.
example: An engineer sizes a heat exchanger for a beverage production line.

label: Food Production
entry_text: Knowledge of techniques and equipment for planting, growing, and harvesting food products (both plant and animal) for consumption, including storage/handling techniques.

label: Food safety
entry_text: Food safety comprises practices and controls that prevent food from harming consumers.
example: A cafeteria keeps raw ingredients separate from prepared salads.

label: Food science
entry_text: Food science studies the composition, properties and behavior of foods during production, storage and use.
example: A team investigates why a sauce separates during refrigerated storage.

label: Forced draft systems
entry_text: Forced draft systems use a fan or blower to push air into equipment that needs controlled airflow.
example: A boiler uses a forced draft fan to supply air for combustion.

label: Foreign Language
entry_text: Knowledge of the structure and content of a foreign (non-English) language including the meaning and spelling of words, rules of composition and grammar, and pronunciation.

label: Forensic dentistry
entry_text: Forensic dentistry applies dental expertise to questions of identification and legal evidence.
example: A specialist compares dental records with available dental evidence to help identify remains.

label: Forklift safety
entry_text: Forklift safety concerns practices that reduce collisions, tip-overs and other injuries during forklift operation.
example: A warehouse uses separate travel lanes for pedestrians and forklifts.

label: Fuel cell
entry_text: A fuel cell converts chemical energy into electricity through an electrochemical reaction while reactants are supplied.
example: A stationary fuel cell supplies backup electricity to a facility.

label: Gas meter systems
entry_text: Gas meter systems measure and record the quantity of gas flowing to a customer or through a process.
example: A utility uses meter readings to calculate monthly consumption.

label: Gastric bypass surgery
entry_text: Gastric bypass surgery alters the digestive tract to reduce stomach capacity and reroute food past part of the small intestine.
example: A bariatric care team monitors nutritional status after gastric bypass.

label: Gemology
entry_text: Gemology is the study and identification of gemstones and their properties.
example: A gemologist distinguishes a natural stone from an imitation by examining its optical properties.

label: General finance
entry_text: General finance concerns how individuals and organizations raise, allocate and manage money and financial risk.
example: A finance team weighs the cost and timing of funding a new facility.

label: General sciences
entry_text: General sciences encompasses foundational knowledge from several scientific disciplines and their methods.
example: A survey course uses chemistry and biology to explain how pond ecosystems function.

label: Generative AI
entry_text: Generative AI uses learned patterns to produce new content such as text, images, audio or code.
example: A designer creates draft layout ideas from a text description.

label: Geographic coordinate system
entry_text: A geographic coordinate system locates positions on a reference surface using angular coordinates, typically latitude and longitude tied to a datum.
example: A map layer uses geographic coordinates to show wildlife observations across several states.

label: Geography
entry_text: Knowledge of principles and methods for describing the features of land, sea, and air masses, including their physical characteristics, locations, interrelationships, and distribution of plant, animal, and human life.

label: Geospatial data
entry_text: Geospatial data describes objects or phenomena with information about their location or spatial extent.
example: A file records flood zones as boundary shapes with estimated risk levels.

label: Geospatial databases
entry_text: Geospatial databases store and query data with geographic or geometric properties.
example: A transit planner queries a database for stops within walking distance of a clinic.

label: Geospatial information technology
entry_text: Geospatial information technology comprises tools and methods for collecting, managing, analyzing and displaying geographically referenced information.
example: An emergency management team combines satellite imagery, mapping software and field observations to track flooding.

label: Government finance
entry_text: Government finance studies how governments raise revenue, manage debt and budget public spending.
example: A city compares tax revenue and bond proceeds when budgeting a transit extension.

label: Graph databases
entry_text: A graph database represents and queries data as entities and relationships, typically expressed as nodes and edges.
example: A travel app finds transfers by following connections among station nodes.

label: Graphics API
entry_text: A graphics API defines programming interfaces for using graphics hardware or a rendering system to create images.
example: A game engine submits commands through Vulkan to render its current scene.

label: Great circle
entry_text: A great circle is the intersection of a sphere with a plane passing through its center.
example: A navigator uses a great-circle arc to estimate the shortest surface route between two airports on a spherical Earth model.

label: Greeks (finance)
entry_text: The Greeks are sensitivity measures for how an option or derivatives portfolio changes with variables such as underlying price, volatility and time.
example: A risk analyst uses delta to estimate a price change from a small move in the underlying asset.

label: Green bond
entry_text: A green bond is debt issued to finance eligible projects with designated environmental benefits.
example: A city allocates green bond proceeds to an energy-efficient transit project.

label: Grieving process
entry_text: The grieving process comprises the varied emotional and practical responses through which people adapt to loss.
example: A bereaved person may alternate between confronting the loss and attending to everyday responsibilities.

label: GSM radio access network
